Why 94% of Flamethrowers Died on Iwo Jima

Out of 380 flamethrower operators deployed on Iwo Jima, only 18 came off the island alive. They had a life expectancy of just 4 minutes on the battlefield. But they were described as both the best and the worst weapon the US Marines had there. Their story, however, is far more horrific than it seems — and now you’re going to see why.

trascrizione_inizio: Out of 380 flamethrower operators deployed on Ioima, only 18 came out of the island alive. They had a life expectancy of just four minutes on the battlefield, but they were described as the best and at the same time the worst weapon US Marines had there. But their story is far more horrific than it seems. And now you're going to see why. When people talk about the Pacific War, they usually mention places like Guadal Canal or Okinawa. But Iima was a different kind of fight altogether. The island itself is only about 8 square miles sitting in the middle of the Pacific between the Maranas and mainland Japan. But in 1945, that small patch of volcanic rock became one of the most valuable pieces of ground in the entire war. The Americans wanted it because of its location. B29 bombers were flying missions from the Maranas to hit targets in Japan, but the route passed right over Ewima. That meant Japanese radar and fighters based there could track and intercept them. Even more importantly, if the US took the island, they could use it as a forward base for fighter escorts, emergency landings, and for launching shorter bombing missions with heavier payloads. The Japanese, of course, knew all of this. They had no illusions about the importance of Eoima, and they fully expected an American invasion. But instead of meeting it head-on at the beach like they had on other islands, they decided to approach this one differently.
